management.value: Management and capital allocation: The company was founded in the 1980s by Scott Cook and Tom Proulx. Cook is a former P&G brand manager who was inspired watching his wife pay household bills by hand. Long before the days of internet banking but when personal computers were becoming popular, he thought computer programs could save people time and resources from doing these types of mundane tasks. He recruited college undergrad Proulx to write the first program for editing, printing and calculating checks. Fast forward a few decades, current chairman and CEO Sasan Goodarzi has been with Intuit since 2011. Prior to the CEO role in 2019, he led their two largest businesses, consumer and global business solutions, and prior to that, he served as Chief Information Officer. In 2019, he declared Intuit’s strategy to be an AI-driven expert platform with data and AI fueling innovation across the company (note that it wasn’t until November 2022 that OpenAI released ChatGPT). Capital allocation priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business for future growth (R&D, AI infrastructure, sales & marketing), 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through the dividend and opportunistic share buybacks, and 3) selective M&A. They initiated the dividend in 2012, they’ve grown the dividend every year since initiating, and they’ve paid out $7.6bn in total dividends over that time frame. Since the early 2000s, they’ve repurchased $25bn in common stock. The M&A track record is mixed. The $7.1bn acquisition of Credit Karma in 2020 has proved to be a good use of capital, whereas the $12.1bn acquisition of Mailchimp in 2021 has not.

terms: Multiple tailwinds driving growth in a large and attractive market
thesis_pillars.text: The shift from 1) in-person assisted tax filing (H&R Block and independent tax preparers) to online and 2) the digitization of SMB financial management, from paper and spreadsheets to cloud-based platforms, are secular tailwinds. AI is also a product catalyst. Intuit sizes the market opportunity at $327bn across SMBs ($186bn) and consumers ($142bn). From a customer standpoint, 300mn are addressable (49mn SMB, 242 consumers). With 10mn SMBs and 86mn consumers today, penetration is 20% and 35%, respectively. The mid-market, currently served by Oracle’s NetSuite and Sage’s Intacct, provides another meaningful future growth opportunity for Intuit.

thesis_pillars.pillar: Dominant position in tax and accounting software with a strong, defensible moat
terms: Dominant position in tax and accounting software with a strong, defensible moat
thesis_pillars.text: On a unitbasis (total number of consumer tax returns filed), Intuit has 25%+ market share in the US. By revenue, share is meaningfully higher (50%+). In US SMB accounting software, their 75% market share has been consistent. Intuit benefits from a rich, proprietary dataset built over 4+ decades. Owning a customers’ complete financial history, including transactions, payroll, invoicing, cash flow, tax statements and lending, makes for a captive customer base. The more time spent and services a customer employs on the platform, the higher the switching costs. IRS integration and commercial relationships with financial institutions, accuracy guarantees and audit support provide barriers to adoption of alternatives. Trust built over 40+ years makes Intuit the low-risk default for high-stakes tax and accounting decisions.
